evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: Bronze 字 shows 子 beneath 宀, raising a child indoors, with 子 also phonetic. Early texts use it for birth and nurture. A Han explanation connects written characters with signs multiplying from earlier forms. Later 字 commonly means a written character.
evidence.title: 字 — historical form and meaning

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education dictionary
evidence.text: Mandarin reading for the child sense: zǐ.
evidence.title: 子 — Mandarin pronunciation

evidence.source: Wiktionary (Zhengzhang pronunciation table)

evidence.title: 子 — Old Chinese pronunciation

evidence.source: CUHK 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.text: The dossier reports that the entry presents a bronze form with 子 below 宀, interpreted as a child under a roof; it assigns 子 both semantic and phonetic value and associates early usage with birth and nurture. I could not independently inspect the entry in this run because the page timed out, so I treat this as a dossier assertion, not fresh verification.
evidence.title: 字 — historical form and meaning

evidence.source: 說文解字注, via Chinese Text Project search result
evidence.text: The search result quotes 許慎’s analysis, “乳也。从子在宀下，子亦聲” and 段玉裁’s expansion: birth/nursing, then 抚字 and written characters; it also quotes the 說文序 explanation that characters multiply through 孳乳. This is a historical account, not independent confirmation of the graphic interpretation. Opening the page returned 403.
evidence.title: 說文解字注（附：六書音均表）: 卷二十八

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Revised Mandarin Dictionary
evidence.field: 孳乳 entry quoting 說文序
evidence.text: Dictionary search result quotes 許慎’s preface: “字者，言孳乳而寖多也” (字 describes forms multiplying by derivation). This establishes a Han-era metalinguistic explanation, not the chronology of 字’s senses. Opening the entry failed in this run.

evidence.source: Unicode Unihan local row cross-checked against official Unicode individual-character records

Official individual record URLs were attempted but returned internal errors; UAX #38 explains Unihan’s database and character lookup conventions.
evidence.title: Unihan Readings; UAX #38 Unicode Han Database

evidence.source: Baxter–Sagart dataset
evidence.text: Exact local entries: 子 *[ts]əʔ and *tsəʔ (variant entries; dataset glosses branch and child/gentleman); 字 *mə-dzə(ʔ)-s (breed/love; character). Preserve the dataset’s notation. The consonant correspondences are compatible with 子 serving as a phonetic element in 字 under this reconstruction, though the readings are not identical and do not alone prove the graphic analysis.
evidence.title: Baxter–Sagart local TSV (upstream page not verified)

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 guide

evidence.field: 字 entry; commentary on senses and formation
evidence.text: The search result reports 段玉裁’s account: 字 originally means giving birth, extended to nurturing and then to written characters; it also reproduces 許慎’s ‘乳也。从子在宀下，子亦聲’ and preface explanation that characters multiply by derivation. evidence.source: Shuowen.org, 說文解字「字」 and 段玉裁注
evidence.field: 字 entry; 說文 definition and 段注
evidence.text: The transmitted 說文 explanation glosses 字 as 乳 (‘give birth/nourish’), analyzes 子 beneath 宀, and says 子 also supplies the sound. 段玉裁 later distinguishes the graphic meeting-of-meaning account from the sound account, and links 乳 to 撫字 and then 文字; he cites the 說文 preface’s explanation that written forms multiply through 孳乳. These are historical lexicographic explanations, not independently dated stages in the word’s semantic history.
evidence.title: 說文解字「字」 — 「說文解字」在線查詢

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction dataset, version 1.1
evidence.field: Dataset rows for 子, 字, 宀
evidence.text: The published table gives 子 *[ts]əʔ (‘1st earthly branch’) and a separate 子 *tsəʔ (‘child; gentleman, master’); 字 is *mə-dzə(ʔ)-s (‘breed, love (v.); character’); 宀 is *me[ŋ] (‘house, building’; marked ‘no pre-Qín exx.’). These are Old Chinese reconstructions in Baxter–Sagart notation. The 子 and 字 consonants are compatible with the traditional sound-component account, but reconstruction alone does not establish the graphic analysis.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

gaps: No independently inspected character-specific paleographic page or glyph image was available; the dossier’s bronze-form description remains unverified in this run.
No secure dated earliest attestation for 字’s birth/nurture sense or written-character sense was located. Do not infer a chronological sequence from lexicographic gloss order.

The semantic path from birth/nurture to writing/character is not established here beyond the Han 說文序’s own derivational explanation that written forms multiply; distinct-root or derivational analyses remain open.
The local Unihan exact rows were checked, but the required official Unicode individual-record click-throughs could not be verified due tool errors.
The local Baxter–Sagart rows were checked, but an upstream versioned dataset page was not verified; notation should be retained exactly as shown in the local TSV.

No evidence found for a whole-graph phonetic borrowing claim; the relevant account is of 子 as a sound component within 字. Dossier claims about Proto-Sino-Tibetan cognates and related words were not verified and are not adopted here.
No corruption or graphic miscopying analysis was found in the inspected material; the record does not establish whether any transmitted form was corrupted.

The 字父己觶 catalog listing supports a Late Shang graph witness, but no inspected inscriptional publication supplied a secure absolute date or contextual reading; the catalog listing does not establish that this is the earliest attestation.

No securely dated early use of 字 for ‘give birth/nurture’ versus ‘written character’ was located. The dictionary gloss ordering and 說文/段注 account do not independently date semantic change. The link between the senses remains an ancient lexicographic explanation, with alternative analyses still unresolved.

The dossier’s common analysis of 宀 as roof/semantic element and 子 as phonetic (and perhaps semantic) is supported here only as the reported 說文 analysis; there was no accessible independent character-specific paleographic study. A research result signals disagreement, but its PDF could not be inspected.

Modern readings verified from Taiwan MOE are 子 zǐ and 字 zì. The exact local Unihan rows were not available in this invocation; both official per-character Unicode lookup URLs returned internal errors, so no Unihan click-through claim is made.

The Baxter–Sagart project PDF was inspected, but its precise rows were not recoverable by search. Do not silently equate dossier transcriptions with the project PDF; the local TSV notation *[ts]əʔ / *tsəʔ for 子 and *mə-dzə(ʔ)-s for 字 remains a local-only report awaiting an exact upstream row check.

Commons description indicates the selected-style candidate is a modern digital redraw and grants CC0, but tool open repeatedly failed and no exact original image URL was verified. Therefore no image candidate is returned. The Sinica page also describes CC0 query-image rights, but its specific 字 image label and direct image URL were not verified.

No evidence for graph corruption or miscopying was established. No whole-graph phonetic borrowing claim was found; 子 is discussed as a proposed sound component within 字. Claims about Proto-Sino-Tibetan cognates and cross-language cognacy remain unverified here.

No independently inspected paleographic specimen or readable character-specific database entry verifies the exact ancient graphic forms of 字. The transmitted 說文 analysis is clear, but its proposed 子 and 宀 roles remain a historical explanation rather than independently confirmed graphic analysis.

The dossier’s identified 字父己觶 witness is not supported by the opened museum record: the record is 父己觶, Western Zhou, and reports only the inscription 父己. No securely read or dated earliest 字 graph witness was established here.

No dated evidence located establishes when 字 was first used with the birth/nurture sense or with the written-character sense, or establishes the transition between them. The 說文 and 段注 provide historical explanations, not a dated semantic sequence.
A scholarly result signals disagreement with the traditional graphic explanation, but the article PDF returned 503; the competing analysis and its evidence remain unknown.

Current Mandarin readings were checked at MOE: 子 zǐ and 字 zì. Official Unicode individual-character lookup pages failed to load; local kMandarin rows are not independently verified click-through evidence in this run.
No graphic corruption or miscopying claim was established. No whole-graph phonetic loan claim was found; the relevant traditional proposal is 子 as a sound component within 字.
Cross-language cognacy proposals and Proto-Sino-Tibetan claims in the dossier were not independently verified and are not adopted.

No usable image of an independently verified early 字 inscription was established in this run. The exact 字 seal-script redraw is well-provenanced and reusable but depicts the transmitted Shuowen seal-script style, not the earlier disputed form history, so no glyph image is proposed.

The Commons original image URL for 字-seal.svg was directly linked from its inspected description page, but the web tool could not fetch the image itself (cache miss); visual inspection was not performed.

The Sinica character endpoint showed 小篆 and 楷書 labels, but no readable specimen metadata establishing a particular dated 字 inscription. Its interface rights notice supports reuse only for images and glyph attributes obtained through that query interface.

A searched 字-bronze-shang.svg Commons page returned cache misses. It is not treated as verified provenance or proposed. The separate 子 oracle image is explicitly a different character and does not establish the component analysis of 字.
